key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: SUDDEN onset within 6-48 hours (acute, NOT chronic). LOCATION: Pain MIGRATES from periumbilical to right lower quadrant (RLQ) over 12-24 hours - highly specific migration pattern. Localizes to McBurney's point in right lower quadrant (RLQ). DURATION: CONSTANT pain lasting hours to days (not episodic). CHARACTER: SHARP and CONSTANT (NOT crampy or intermittent). AGGRAVATING: WORSENS WITH MOVEMENT - patients can't jump, cough, or tolerate car bumps. Lying still required. RELIEVING: Lying motionless provides slight relief. NOTHING fully relieves pain. Movement worsens it. TIMING: CONSTANT and progressively worsening over time (not waves). SEVERITY: 7-10/10, moderate to severe. ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: ANOREXIA in >90% (ask 'are you hungry?' - 'yes' makes appendicitis unlikely), nausea and vomiting (AFTER pain onset), low-grade fever (100-102°F). KEY POSITIVES: Anorexia, right lower quadrant (RLQ) tenderness, periumbilical→RLQ migration. KEY NEGATIVES: Pain starting in right lower quadrant (RLQ) without migration is less typical. CRAMPY pain suggests obstruction. PROFUSE WATERY DIARRHEA suggests gastroenteritis. High fever >103°F suggests perforation.

includes.patient_friendly: all at once or very quickly
lower right side around your groin

red_flags: Sudden severe pain that then improves briefly - may indicate PERFORATION
Severe pain with abdominal rigidity (board-like abdomen) - perforation with peritonitis, call 911
High fever >103°F with severe pain - possible perforation
Hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status - septic shock, call 911
